mcp.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
mcp.description: The standard protocol AI agents use to reach external tools and data
mcp.conceptDesc: MCP is a standard protocol that connects AI agents to external systems such as databases, browsers, and external APIs. An MCP server provides tools (functions the agent can run), resources (data it can read), and prompts (reusable prompts), and the agent (the client) calls them. Local processes connect over stdio, and remote servers connect over Streamable HTTP.

visualizer.description: AI agents reach external services (databases, browsers, GitHub, and more) through MCP servers.

mcp.specIntro: The latest revision of the MCP spec is 2026-07-28. Compared with the previous revision (2025-11-25), the basic structure of the protocol changed, so check the revision when you build a server or follow an older example.
specChanges: Stateless protocol: the initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta
server/discover added: an RPC that advertises the versions and capabilities a server supports, which servers must implement
Tasks moved out of the core protocol into an official extension
Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated. They keep working during the deprecation window, but new implementations should not use them
The HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated and should be migrated to Streamable HTTP. stdio stays as is

servers.name: GitHub
servers.desc: Issues, PRs, and code search (GitHub's official remote server)

servers.name: Chrome DevTools
servers.desc: Console, network, and performance trace debugging (Chromium only)

servers.name: DBHub
servers.desc: Querying PostgreSQL and other databases (use a read-only account)

servers.name: Sentry

mcp.configInfoTitle: Where a server is stored depends on its scope
mcp.configInfoDesc: In Claude Code you add servers with the claude mcp add command. The default local scope is a private setting for the current project, stored in ~/.claude.json. The project scope is stored in .mcp.json at the project root and shared with your team through git. The user scope applies to all your projects. Servers from .mcp.json need approval the first time they are used, and tokens should be injected with ${VAR} environment variable expansion instead of being written into the file.
tips: Connect only the servers a project needs, and turn off unused ones in /mcp
MCP tool definitions are deferred by default, so only tool names and server instructions enter context, but for tools that have a CLI, such as gh, the CLI uses less context
Connect databases with a read-only account, and never connect directly to a production DB
Switch older configs that use the SSE transport to the HTTP transport
mcp.addCode:
# Remote server (HTTP) — GitHub's official MCP server
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/

# Local server (stdio) — everything after `--` is the server command
claude mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest

# Share with the team: project scope → saved to .mcp.json at the project root
claude mcp add --scope project context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp

# Manage
claude mcp list
claude mcp remove playwright
# Inside a session, /mcp shows status, runs OAuth, and toggles servers

skillsHooks.title: Skills and Hooks
skillsHooks.description: Procedural knowledge that loads only when needed, and event automation that always runs
skillsHooks.skillsInfoDesc: A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches the agent the procedure and knowledge for a specific kind of task. Claude reads each skill's description and loads the skill on its own when the task is relevant, and you can also invoke it directly with /skill-name. The body enters context only when the skill is actually used, so long reference material costs almost nothing the rest of the time. The older custom slash commands (.claude/commands) have been merged into skills, and the skill format follows the Agent Skills open standard, so skills can be reused in other tools.

skillExamples.name: /code-review
skillExamples.desc: Reviews the current diff or a PR for bugs

skillExamples.name: /simplify
skillExamples.desc: Cleans up duplication and complexity in changed code

skillExamples.name: /loop
skillExamples.desc: Runs a prompt or command repeatedly on an interval

skillExamples.name: /run
skillExamples.desc: Launches the app to confirm a change actually works

skillFields.name: description
skillFields.desc: What the skill does and when to use it. Claude uses this to decide whether to load it

skillFields.name: disable-model-invocation
skillFields.desc: When true, only you can invoke it. Use for tasks with side effects such as deploys

skillFields.name: allowed-tools
skillFields.desc: Tools pre-approved during the turn that invokes the skill

skillFields.name: context: fork
skillFields.desc: Runs the skill in a separate subagent to protect the main context

skillsHooks.hooksInfoDesc: A hook is a handler that runs automatically when a lifecycle event occurs in the agent. Instructions in CLAUDE.md are only context the agent consults, but a hook always runs when its condition matches, so hooks are how you enforce rules that can't have exceptions. A command hook receives the event data as JSON on stdin, and returning exit code 2 blocks the action. Note that any other error code, including 1, is treated as a non-blocking error and the action still proceeds.

hookTypes.name: SessionStart
hookTypes.timing: When a session starts or resumes

hookTypes.name: UserPromptSubmit
hookTypes.timing: Right after a prompt is submitted, before processing

hookTypes.name: Notification
hookTypes.usage: Forwarding to desktop or chat notifications

skillsHooks.hookTypesNote: There are more than 30 events in total, including SubagentStop, SessionEnd, and PermissionRequest. Besides shell commands (command), hook types include http, mcp_tool, prompt, and the experimental agent.
skillsHooks.claudeMdInfoDesc: CLAUDE.md is a project instruction file loaded at the start of every session. Put in it what can't be learned from the code alone: build and test commands, code conventions, and rules that must be followed. It always takes up context, so keep it under 200 lines, move procedures needed only for specific tasks into skills, and move rules that apply only to certain paths into .claude/rules/. The /init command generates a first draft. If you use several tools, keep the instructions in the standard AGENTS.md file. Claude Code (v2.1.277 or later) reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md, and reads only CLAUDE.md when both exist.
skillsHooks.skillCode:
<!-- .claude/skills/create-component/SKILL.md -->
---
name: create-component
description: Creates a React component that follows project conventions. Use when the user asks for a new component.
argument-hint: [component-name]
---

Create the $ARGUMENTS component.

1. Find a similar component in src/components and check its pattern
2. Create the component file (kebab-case) following that pattern
3. Create a test file alongside it
4. Update the barrel export (index.ts)
5. Verify with bun run typecheck and bun run test
skillsHooks.hookScriptCode:
#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/format.sh — input arrives as JSON on stdin
FILE=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')
npx prettier --write "$FILE"

#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh
COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  echo "rm -rf is blocked by a hook" >&2
  exit 2   # 2 = block. exit 1 does not block
fi
exit 0
skillsHooks.claudeMdCode:
<!-- CLAUDE.md -->
# E-commerce Platform

## Commands
- `bun run dev`: dev server
- `bun run typecheck`: type check
- `bun run test`: tests

## Conventions
- File names use kebab-case
- Server components by default; mark client ones with 'use client'
- Types live in src/types; prefer interface

## Must follow
- Make typecheck and test pass after every change
- Never read or modify .env files

@AGENTS.md

agentMode.title: Agent Mode in Practice
agentMode.description: Using permission modes, plan mode, subagents, and agent teams where each one fits
agentMode.permissionModesInfoTitle: The switch for how much you delegate
agentMode.permissionModesInfoDesc: A permission mode decides which actions the agent can take without your approval. Switch modes during a session with Shift+Tab, or set one at startup with the --permission-mode option.

permissionModes.name: default (Manual)
permissionModes.desc: Asks every time before file edits and shell commands

permissionModes.name: acceptEdits
permissionModes.desc: Auto-approves file edits, asks for everything else

permissionModes.name: plan
permissionModes.desc: Reads and explores only; does not edit source files

permissionModes.name: auto
permissionModes.desc: A classifier reviews risky actions instead of you

permissionModes.name: dontAsk
permissionModes.desc: Runs only pre-approved tools and denies the rest

permissionModes.name: bypassPermissions
permissionModes.desc: Skips all checks. Use only in isolated environments

agentMode.planModeInfoDesc: Start in plan mode for work with a wide impact, such as large refactors or new features. The agent only reads code while it proposes an approach, and implements after you approve. This cuts the cost of redoing work that went ahead in the wrong direction.
agentMode.subAgentsInfoTitle: Helpers that work in their own context
agentMode.subAgentsInfoDesc: A subagent works in a context separate from the main conversation and returns only a summarized result. Hand it tasks with long output, such as exploration or test runs, and the main context stays clean. Define roles you use often as Markdown files under .claude/agents/ and reuse them.

subAgents.name: Explore
subAgents.desc: Read-only. File discovery, code search, and codebase analysis

subAgents.name: Plan
subAgents.desc: Read-only. Does the research a plan needs during plan mode

subAgents.name: general-purpose
subAgents.desc: Complex tasks that need both exploration and changes

subAgents.name: Custom agents
subAgents.desc: Define tools, model, and prompt yourself in .claude/agents/*.md

agentMode.cursorInfoDesc: Cursor's project rules are defined as .mdc files in the .cursor/rules folder. Depending on the alwaysApply, description, and globs frontmatter, a rule works in one of four ways: always applied, applied when the agent judges it relevant, applied to specific files, or applied manually with an @-mention. Cursor also reads AGENTS.md at the project root and in subdirectories.
agentMode.interviewModeInfoTitle: When requirements are fuzzy, let the agent ask
agentMode.interviewModeInfoDesc: Interviewing is a prompt pattern, not a separate mode or flag. If you haven't worked out what to build yet, ask the agent to interview you until it could write the spec. The agent asks multiple-choice questions about each undecided part, then writes up a spec document once the answers add up.
agentMode.interviewModeTipDesc: Once the spec document is done, start the build in a fresh session. You begin with a clean context and a written definition of done, without the long interview conversation, and the same document serves as the reference for review later.
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsTitle: Subagents or Agent Teams: Which and When
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsCompareTitle: Subagent Delegation vs Agent Team Collaboration
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsSimulationTitle: Compare the subagent and agent team flows step by step
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsReadyHint: Start: press Next step to see how each approach proceeds.
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsIntro: Both parallelize work, but they communicate differently. Subagents report results only to the main agent, while agent team teammates watch a shared task list and message each other directly.
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsPrompt: Same task: find the cause of an intermittently failing login bug
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsParallelTitle: Subagents: delegation that returns only results
teamsVsSubAgentsParallelItems: The main agent splits the investigation into independent units
Subagents investigate in parallel, each in its own context
Each subagent returns only a summarized result to the main agent
The main agent combines the results and decides on the cause
teamsVsSubAgentsTeamsItems: The lead puts one task per hypothesis on the shared task list and spawns teammates
Teammates claim tasks and test hypotheses in their own independent sessions
Teammates message each other directly to challenge hypotheses and share findings
The lead synthesizes the surviving hypotheses and shuts the teammates down
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsParallelToken: Lower token cost: only summarized results return to the main context
agentMode.teamsVsSubAgentsTeamsToken: Higher token cost: each teammate runs as a separate Claude instance
agentMode.teamsCompareTitle: With and Without an Agent Team
agentMode.teamsDescription: Agent teams are an experimental feature in which several Claude Code sessions collaborate as one team, and they are off by default. The lead session splits the work and hands it to teammates, and each teammate works in its own context and talks to the others directly. The same request proceeds differently with a team on or off.
agentMode.teamsSharedPromptText: Review PR #142 for security, performance, and test coverage.
teamsWithGenerative: The lead registers one review task per perspective on the shared task list
Security, performance, and testing teammates review at the same time in independent sessions
Teammates exchange messages and examine each other's findings
The lead combines the three perspectives and reports
teamsWithoutGenerative: One session reads the whole PR
It reviews security, performance, and testing one after another
If needed, it hands part of the investigation to a subagent and gets a summary back
It organizes the results within a single context and reports
agentMode.teamsWithGenerativeToken: High token usage: grows with the number of teammates, about 7x a standard session when teammates run in plan mode
agentMode.teamsWithoutGenerativeToken: Low token usage: the more efficient choice for sequential work or edits to the same file
teamsGuide: A good fit for work teammates can do independently: research and review, building separate modules, debugging with competing hypotheses
For sequential work, edits to the same file, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents work better
Start with 3 to 5 teammates, and give each teammate different files to avoid conflicts
It is experimental and has limitations, such as in-process teammates not being restored when you resume a session

tokenOptimization.title: Saving Tokens and Optimizing Context
tokenOptimization.description: Habits that keep context small, and how to pick browser automation tools by cost
tokenOptimization.playwrightMigrationTitle: Moving from Playwright MCP to Playwright CLI
tokenOptimization.playwrightMigrationInfoDesc: Playwright MCP returns the page's accessibility snapshot and screenshots in its responses, so that content piles up in context. The agent-oriented Playwright CLI (@playwright/cli) saves the same results to files and returns only the path, so the agent reads just the parts it needs. The Playwright team also says the CLI is the better fit for coding agents that can use a shell. The savings vary widely with how you measure, so check with /context yourself rather than trusting a specific multiplier.
tokenOptimization.playwrightTip1: Exploratory automation, self-healing tests, and long-running workflows that need persistent browser state
tokenOptimization.playwrightTip2: Everyday page checks and E2E verification by coding agents that have a shell and file system
tokenOptimization.playwrightTip3: Keep screenshots and traces only at the point of failure
tokenOptimization.playwrightTip4: Save long logs to a file and give the agent only a summary and the path
tokenOptimization.playwrightTip5: Lock checked scenarios into test code, and verify with playwright test from then on
tokenOptimization.mcpVsCdpTitle: Choosing a Browser Tool: Playwright and Chrome DevTools MCP
tokenOptimization.mcpVsCdpIntro: Playwright is strong at reproducing and verifying user flows. Chrome DevTools MCP, built on CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol), is strong at debugging that looks inside the browser: console, network, and performance traces.

mcpVsCdpRows.mcp: Automating user flows such as clicks and input, and E2E tests
mcpVsCdpRows.cdp: Analyzing console errors, network requests, and performance traces
mcpVsCdpRows.note: Playwright to verify features, DevTools to find causes
Playwright when you need cross-browser checks

mcpVsCdpRows.mcp: MCP puts snapshots into context; the CLI saves them to files
mcpVsCdpRows.cdp: Many tools, so its tool list takes up more context while connected
mcpVsCdpRows.note: Connect only for the work that needs it

mcpVsCdpRows.mcp: Scenarios kept as test code and rerun in CI
mcpVsCdpRows.cdp: Centered on interactive debugging, so results are hard to keep as code

tokenOptimization.contextOptimizationInfoTitle: The basic principle for cutting cost
tokenOptimization.contextOptimizationInfoDesc: Token cost scales with context size. The agent resends the whole conversation with every request, so in a session left open all day, even a one-line question is processed together with everything accumulated so far. Keeping context small is the most effective saving.
contextOptimizationChecklist: Start fresh with /clear when you move to unrelated work
Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, and move task-specific instructions into skills
Hand tasks with long output, such as test runs or log analysis, to subagents
For tools that have a CLI (gh, aws, and so on), use the CLI instead of MCP, and turn off unused MCP servers
Handle most work with a lighter model, and save the top model and high effort for complex design
Vague requests trigger broad exploration. Spell out the files, scope, and done criteria
If the direction is wrong, stop right away with Esc and go back with /rewind

promptEngineering.title: Advanced Prompt Engineering
promptEngineering.description: Telling the agent what it can't see, and giving it criteria to verify its own work
promptEngineering.goalOrientedTitle: Prompts Built on Goals and Done Criteria
promptEngineering.goalOrientedDesc: The agent can find the procedure on its own. What you need to supply is the goal, the scope, and a way to tell when it's done.
promptEngineering.contextInfoTitle: Tell the agent what it can't see
promptEngineering.contextInfoDesc: The agent can read the code in the repository, but not the background knowledge in your head. Point at the relevant files with @, and pass along the existing pattern to follow, constraints that don't show in the code, and the full error message with how to reproduce it. Unnecessary exploration drops and results get more accurate.
promptEngineering.constraintsInfoTitle: Give it a way to check itself
promptEngineering.constraintsInfoDesc: Give the agent something it can run to verify its work, such as test cases, expected output, or screenshots, and it finds and fixes problems before you have to point them out. It is an effective way to raise the quality of the result.
promptEngineering.iterativeInfoTitle: Refine step by step, correct course early
promptEngineering.iterativeInfoDesc: Refine complex work step by step: the big picture, then the implementation details, then the edge cases. When the agent starts heading the wrong way, stopping and going back right away costs less than waiting. Don't keep piling unrelated tasks into one session; clear the context when the task changes.
promptEngineering.badCode:

# Dictating every step

 2. Then find the function
 3. Add types"

workflows.title: Real-World Workflows
workflows.description: Feature development, bug fixes, code review, and automation that runs without you
workflows.featureDevInfoDesc: Work in this order: explore, plan, implement, verify, review, commit. Agree on the direction during planning, and have the agent verify with type checks and tests at each implementation step, so there is less to fix all at once at the end.
workflows.bugFixInfoDesc: Give the full error message along with how to reproduce it, and have the agent reproduce the bug with a failing test first. The test turning green is the evidence of the fix.
workflows.automationInfoTitle: Runs that don't need you watching
workflows.automationInfoDesc: claude -p is headless mode: it runs once without a conversation and exits, which suits CI and scripts. When several tasks run at once, use worktrees to give each session its own working directory so their changes don't mix. Send long-running work to a background session and check its progress in agent view.
tips: Connect PR creation and review through the gh CLI or the GitHub MCP server
Turn recurring team procedures (commit rules, release checks) into project skills and share them
For unattended runs, narrow what is allowed ahead of time with permission rules

verification.title: Verification and Safe Use
verification.description: Verifying AI-generated code, managing permissions, handling prompt injection, and team guidelines
verification.autoVerifyInfoDesc: A PostToolUse hook can run lint or type checks every time a file is modified. When a check fails, exit with code 2 and write the errors to stderr; they are passed to the agent, which fixes them itself. To force the full test suite when the agent finishes, use a Stop hook.
checklist: Does the business logic match the requirements?
Is it consistent with existing code patterns?
Are there security vulnerabilities? (input validation, authn/authz)
Does it use packages or APIs that don't exist?
Are there performance problems? (N+1, memory leaks)
Do the tests verify real behavior? (not tests written only to pass)
verification.permissionsInfoDesc: Write per-tool rules under permissions in settings.json to set what is allowed. Rules are evaluated in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first match decides the outcome, so an allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule. Commit them to the project's .claude/settings.json and the whole team uses the same rules.
verification.injectionDesc: Web pages, issue bodies, and MCP tool responses that the agent reads can hide instructions meant to trick it. Content that comes from outside must be treated as data, not instructions, and you should not install MCP servers, skills, or plugins from unknown sources. Block files that hold secrets with deny rules, and use bypassPermissions mode, which skips all checks, only in isolated environments.

required.title: Required Checks
items: A person reviews all AI-generated code before merge
Security-related code needs senior developer approval
Confirm the full test suite passes before production deploys

prohibited.title: Prohibited
items: Putting secret keys or personal data in prompts
Connecting MCP directly to a production DB
Installing MCP servers, skills, or plugins from unknown sources

verification.importantNoteDesc: However capable AI agents become, final responsibility always lies with the developer. Review all AI-generated code before you commit it.
